I plan to plant at LEAST 4 trees over the next year in our backyard farther around the perimeter of the lot and would be happy to send the city photos of the new trees to eventually replace the dangerous trees so close to the home.

tree_description: Very large white oak with fungus.
comments: Microscopic examination of the submitted sample revealed the oak bracket fungus, Pseudoinonotus dryadeus. This decay fungus is found near the base of oak and true fir trees. This fungus is closely related to and was previously classified within Inonotus, many of which can cause extensive decay of the trunk, root flare, and buttress roots.?This is a white rot which may reduce structural integrity by degrading lignin and/or cellulose. This fungus may grow alone or in clusters and is generally present between summer and fall. The fruiting bodies of this fungus have an amorphous shape, a light yellow/buff color of the surface, and golden droplets along the surface.

trees.comments: Undesirable, invasive species. One major scaffold limb is in contact with Tree 2, resulting in a rub condition. The extent of any resulting damage to Tree 1 is not fully visible from the inspection vantage point. Size is approximate.

trees.tree_description: Numbered flagging tape
trees.comments: Co-dominant structure is present at both the lower and upper bole areas, with acute unions exhibiting included bark. One primary leader has failed and broken off, with associated decay and wood loss at the former attachment point. Remaining structure includes a dog-legged scaffold branch at the point of former leader failure. A longitudinal fusiform canker is present on the opposing leader, visible from the east side. The canker appears deeply incised with pronounced woundwood formation consistent with a ram’s horn pattern. The defect is located along a gentle bending moment on the tension side of the stem, indicating elevated structural concern at that location. A rub wound is present on the same side of the stem as the canker, located on the south side of the tree and associated with conflict from Tree 1; full extent of the wound is partially obscured. The tree shares a deformed, shared structural root plate with Trees 3 and 4.

trees.tree_description: Numbered flagging tape
trees.comments: From a physiological standpoint, the tree appears healthy with no significant canopy decline observed. However, the tree shares a deformed structural root plate with Trees 2 and 4. In the event of approval and subsequent removal of Tree 2, there will be a loss of shared structural root support, resulting in reduced anchorage, increased risk of instability, and increased susceptibility to wind throw due to newly exposed conditions.

trees.tree_description: Numbered flagging tape
trees.comments: Similar to Tree 3, the tree appears physiologically healthy. However, it exhibits poor structural form with a bowed, asymmetrical canopy and a highly suppressed growth habit. The tree shares a deformed, shared structural root plate with Trees 2 and 3. In the event of removal of adjacent tree or trees, there will be a loss of shared structural root support.

trees.tree_description: Numbered flagging tape
trees.comments: Tree exhibits an asymmetrical, phototropic canopy with a noticeable lean over the adjacent dwelling’s roof system, resulting in an unbalanced crown. A longitudinal fusiform canker is present on the rear tension side of the stem, located on the west side of the trunk at mid-bole, with visible disruption to the sapwood and pronounced wound development. The location on the tension side, combined with canopy imbalance and lean, indicates elevated structural concern and increased potential for stem failure under load.

trees.tree_description: Numbered flagging tape
trees.comments: The tree exhibits a deformed structural root plate in direct association with the adjacent retaining wall. Cavities and decay are present at the base within buttress roots, including open voids. Review of imagery from 2012 to 2014 indicates localized reconstruction of the retaining wall in this area, with mismatched stone patterning and newer mortar suggesting prior disturbance. These conditions indicate compromised root integrity and reduced anchorage at a critical load-bearing zone, with elevated potential for root plate failure. Removal of adjacent larger pines, particularly Trees 2, 3, and 5, would significantly increase site wind exposure and loading on this tree. Observed conditions do not indicate that the tree is well-suited to accommodate this increased exposure.

trees.tree_description: Numbered flagging tape
trees.comments: ree appears to have originated as a basal sprout, resulting in a once co-dominant structure. A prior co-dominant leader has been removed or failed, leaving a large wound site with callus development and a small residual cavity that appears partially closed but continues to function as a moisture-collecting point. The lower wound area has developed into a dog-legged form. Upper to mid-bole bark sloughing is present, observed via zoom photography. The underlying cause could not be fully determined during inspection; however, the condition is noted as an additional concern. Percussive sounding with a mallet around the wound site produced hollow tones at locations documented in the photo set, suggesting internal voids or decay. The canopy exhibits an asymmetrical form, resulting in an uneven load distribution directed toward adjacent properties. Targets present within the fall zone include neighboring dwellings and outdoor living areas, including a children’s play area.

trees.comments: A previous pruning cut was made into the trunk wood of the main parent stem, and a seam is visible below this cut. Both of these defects are present below the main canopy load. Like Tree #1, removal is recommended, as alternative mitigation is not sufficient to reduce risk.

A leader (more than 30% of the canopy) failed on the left side (see photo), and the resulting damage has affected the main parent stem. Because of the extent of canopy loss and stem damage, removal is recommended as the only effective risk mitigation.
